claim: Lactate oxidation with NAD+ as electron acceptor is a highly endergonic reaction.
source: Lactate oxidation with NAD+ as electron acceptor is a highly endergonic reaction.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical knowledge about the thermodynamics of lactate oxidation.

claim: Some anaerobic bacteria overcome the energetic hurdle of lactate oxidation by flavin-based electron bifurcation/confurcation (FBEB/FBEC) using a lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh) in concert with the electron-transferring proteins EtfA and EtfB.
source: Some anaerobic bacteria overcome the energetic hurdle by flavin-based electron bifurcation/confurcation (FBEB/FBEC) using a lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh) in concert with the electron-transferring proteins EtfA and EtfB.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The (Ldh-EtfAB)2 complex of Acetobacterium woodii was characterized by electron cryo-microscopy at 2.43 Å resolution.
source: The electron cryo-microscopically characterized (Ldh-EtfAB)2 complex of Acetobacterium woodii at 2.43 Å resolution consists of a mobile EtfAB shuttle domain located between the rigid central Ldh and the peripheral EtfAB base units.
evidence: The resolution is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the cryo-EM data in Table 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The (Ldh-EtfAB)2 complex consists of a mobile EtfAB shuttle domain located between the rigid central Ldh and the peripheral EtfAB base units.
source: The electron cryo-microscopically characterized (Ldh-EtfAB)2 complex of Acetobacterium woodii at 2.43 Å resolution consists of a mobile EtfAB shuttle domain located between the rigid central Ldh and the peripheral EtfAB base units.
evidence: This structural observation is directly stated and supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: The FADs of Ldh and the EtfAB shuttle domain contact each other thereby forming the D (dehydrogenation-connected) state.
source: The FADs of Ldh and the EtfAB shuttle domain contact each other thereby forming the D (dehydrogenation-connected) state.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The intermediary Glu37 and Glu139 may harmonize the redox potentials between the FADs and the pyruvate/lactate pair crucial for FBEC.
source: The intermediary Glu37 and Glu139 may harmonize the redox potentials between the FADs and the pyruvate/lactate pair crucial for FBEC.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural observations shown in Figure 9B.

claim: A plausible novel B (bifurcation-connected) state was obtained by integrating Alphafold2 calculations.
source: By integrating Alphafold2 calculations a plausible novel B (bifurcation-connected) state was obtained allowing electron transfer between the EtfAB base and shuttle FADs.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold2 as described in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The B state allows electron transfer between the EtfAB base and shuttle FADs.
source: By integrating Alphafold2 calculations a plausible novel B (bifurcation-connected) state was obtained allowing electron transfer between the EtfAB base and shuttle FADs.
evidence: This is inferred from the AlphaFold2-derived structure showing appropriate distances for electron transfer.

claim: Kinetic analysis of enzyme variants suggests a correlation between NAD+ binding site and D-to-B-state transition implicating a 75° rotation of the EtfAB shuttle domain.
source: Kinetic analysis of enzyme variants suggests a correlation between NAD+ binding site and D-to-B-state transition implicating a 75° rotation of the EtfAB shuttle domain.
evidence: This is based on kinetic data from enzyme variants shown in Table 2 and structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The FBEC inactivity when truncating the ferredoxin domain of EtfA substantiates its role as redox relay.
source: The FBEC inactivity when truncating the ferredoxin domain of EtfA substantiates its role as redox relay.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data from the ΔFe/S and ΔFe/S-arm variants shown in Table 2.

claim: Lactate oxidation in Ldh is assisted by the catalytic base His423 and a metal center.
source: Lactate oxidation in Ldh is assisted by the catalytic base His423 and a metal center.
evidence: This is based on structural observations shown in Figure 6B and comparison with related enzymes.

claim: Anaerobic energy metabolisms frequently operate at the thermodynamic limit of life.
source: Anaerobic energy metabolisms frequently operate at the thermodynamic limit of life.
evidence: This is a general statement of established knowledge in microbial bioenergetics.

claim: Various microorganisms developed early in evolution an energy-coupling process termed flavin-based electron bifurcation/confurcation (FBEB/FBEC) embedded into a modular, mostly soluble enzyme complex.
source: For energy yield optimization, various microorganisms developed early in evolution an energy-coupling process termed flavin-based electron bifurcation/confurcation (FBEB/FBEC) embedded into a modular, mostly soluble enzyme complex (Buckel and Thauer, 2013; Herrmann et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008; Müller et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In FBEB, an endergonic reduction, normally of oxidized ferredoxin (Fdox), is driven by a simultaneous exergonic reduction.
source: In the more familiar FBEB direction, an endergonic reduction, normally of oxidized ferredoxin (Fdox), is driven by a simultaneous exergonic reduction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the general mechanism of FBEB as illustrated in Figure 1A and is established knowledge.

claim: The reversible bifurcating hydrogenase oxidizes hydrogen gas to two protons and two single split electrons that are transferred to NAD(P)+ and Fdox.
source: One example is the reversible bifurcating hydrogenase (Katsyv et al., 2021; Schuchmann and Müller, 2012; Schut and Adams, 2009; Wang et al., 2013) that oxidizes hydrogen gas to two protons and two single split electrons; the latter are transferred to the two-electron acceptors, NAD(P)+ and Fdox.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work on bifurcating hydrogenases.

claim: In the confurcation mode H2 is produced from reduced ferredoxin (Fdred) and NAD(P)H.
source: In the confurcation mode H2 is produced from reduced ferredoxin (Fdred) and NAD(P)H (Katsyv et al., 2021; Schuchmann and Müller, 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on confurcating hydrogenases.

claim: A flavin endowed with an extremely inverted one-electron redox potential serves as key player for energy coupling in FBEB/FBEC.
source: As key player for energy coupling in FBEB/FBEC serves a flavin endowed with an extremely inverted one-electron redox potential implicating a very short-living FAD•– state (Duan et al., 2021; Lubner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on flavin redox properties.

claim: The flavin involved in FBEB/FBEC has a very short-living FAD•– state.
source: As key player for energy coupling in FBEB/FBEC serves a flavin endowed with an extremely inverted one-electron redox potential implicating a very short-living FAD•– state (Duan et al., 2021; Lubner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on flavin radical intermediates.

claim: One-electron redox potentials of E(FAD/FAD•–) = –911 mV and E(FAD•–/FADH–) = +359 mV are experimentally determined for the bifurcating NADPH dependent Fdox:NAD+ oxidoreductase.
source: One-electron redox potentials of E(FAD/FAD•–) = –911 mV and E(FAD•–/FADH–) = +359 mV are experimentally determined for the bifurcating NADPH dependent Fdox:NAD+ oxidoreductase (Lubner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a specific experimental measurement cited from previous work.

claim: Strongly inverted one-electron redox potentials are reported for quinones in the related quinone-based electron bifurcation process embedded into the bc1 complex.
source: Strongly inverted one-electron redox potentials are also reported for quinones in the related quinone-based electron bifurcation process embedded into the bc1 complex (Crofts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on quinone redox chemistry.

claim: The electron-confurcating Ldh-EtfAB complex catalyzes the endergonic oxidation of lactate to pyruvate with NAD+ as electron acceptor driven by simultaneous co-oxidation of Fdred.
source: The electron-confurcating lactate dehydrogenase/electron-transferring flavoprotein (Ldh-EtfAB) complex, the research subject of this report, catalyzes the endergonic oxidation of lactate to the central cellular metabolite pyruvate (Bock et al., 1994; Dönig and Müller, 2018; Kandler, 1983) with NAD+ as electron acceptor driven by simultaneous co-oxidation of Fdred (Figure 1B; Weghoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The FBEC reaction of Ldh-EtfAB occurs in anaerobic sulfate-reducing and acetogenic bacteria.
source: This FBEC reaction occurs in anaerobic sulfate-reducing and acetogenic bacteria (Vita et al., 2015; Weghoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on bacterial metabolism.

claim: Lactate is accumulated in huge amounts as intermediate during anaerobic glucose degradation via glycolysis to the endproduct acetate.
source: Lactate is accumulated in huge amounts as intermediate during anaerobic glucose degradation via glycolysis to the endproduct acetate (Müller, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on anaerobic metabolism.

claim: The confurcating Ldh-EtfAB complex belongs to the bEtf family, the largest and most diverse group of FBEB/FBEC enzymes.
source: The confurcating Ldh-EtfAB complex belongs to the bEtf family, the largest and most diverse group of FBEB/FBEC enzymes (Buckel and Thauer, 2018a).
evidence: This is a classification statement supported by a citation.

claim: bEtf family members are built up of a variable dehydrogenase/oxidoreductase core and several peripherally attached EtfAB modules.
source: bEtf family members are built up of a variable dehydrogenase/oxidoreductase core and several peripherally attached EtfAB modules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Demmer et al., 2018; Demmer et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The EtfAB heterodimer is built up of an EtfAB base composed of the N-terminal segments of EtfA and EtfB (termed domains I and III, respectively) and a module termed domain II or EtfAB shuttle domain.
source: The EtfAB heterodimer is built up of an EtfAB base composed of the N-terminal segments of EtfA and EtfB (termed domains I and III, respectively) and a module termed domain II or EtfAB shuttle domain (due to its shuttling role between two sites far away from each other) formed by the tightly associated C-terminal segment of EtfA and the C-terminal arm of EtfB (Chowdhury et al., 2014).
evidence: This structural description is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The rigid oxidoreductase core and EtfAB base platforms and the mobile EtfAB shuttle domain each carry one FAD termed d-FAD, b-FAD and a-FAD.
source: Both the rigid oxidoreductase core and EtfAB base platforms and the mobile EtfAB shuttle domain carry one FAD termed d-FAD, b-FAD and a-FAD.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure and previous work.

claim: In the bEtf family, a-FAD transfers electrons between the bifurcating b-FAD and the distant d-FAD.
source: In the bEtf family, a-FAD transfers electrons between the bifurcating b-FAD and the distant d-FAD, the site of the weak electron donor (Demmer et al., 2018; Demmer et al., 2017) thereby creating the B (bifurcation-connected) and D (dehydrogenation-connected) states.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and mechanistic work.

claim: The rotating EtfAB shuttle domain is joined with the EtfAB base by two mobile linkers and held in a defined trajectory under participation of two segments termed EtfB protrusion and EtfA hairpin.
source: The rotating EtfAB shuttle domain joined with the EtfAB base by two mobile linkers is held in a defined trajectory under participation of two segments termed EtfB protrusion and EtfA hairpin (Demmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work.

claim: Some EtfA family members contain an N-terminal Fd domain carrying one or two [4Fe-4S] clusters to mediate electron transfer between the external Fd and the bifurcating FAD.
source: Some EtfA family members contain an N-terminal Fd domain carrying one or two [4Fe-4S] clusters (Demmer et al., 2018) to mediate electron transfer (ET) between the external Fd and the bifurcating FAD.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and structural observations.

claim: Ldh-EtfAB possesses a Fd domain with one [4Fe-4S] cluster based on sequence and signature motif (C(x)17CxxCxxC).
source: Deduced from the sequence and the signature motif (C(x)17CxxCxxC) Ldh-EtfAB possesses a Fd domain with one [4Fe-4S] cluster (Weghoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: The encoding strep-tagged lctBCD genes from A. woodii were cloned into the expression vector pET21a and expressed in E. coli strain BL21(DE3)ΔiscR.
source: For structural and functional analysis, the encoding strep-tagged lctBCD genes from A. woodii were cloned into the expression vector pET21a and expressed in the Escherichia coli strain BL21(DE3)ΔiscR (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The Ldh-EtfAB complex was purified under anoxic conditions by strep-tactin affinity and Superdex 200 size exclusion chromatography.
source: The Ldh-EtfAB complex was purified under anoxic conditions by strep-tactin affinity and Superdex 200 size exclusion chromatography.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: A denaturing gel showed three distinct proteins with apparent molecular masses of 51 kDa (LDH), 46 kDa (EtfA), and 29 kDa (EtfB) that match the predicted gene masses of 51.2 kDa, 46.2 kDa, and 29.1 kDa.
source: A denaturating gel showed three distinct proteins with apparent molecular masses of 51 kDa (LDH), 46 kDa (EtfA), and 29 kDa (EtfB) (Figure 2A) that matches to the predicted gene masses of 51.2 kDa, 46.2 kDa, and 29.1 kDa.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Native gel electrophoresis and analytical gel filtration data revealed a rather fragile multimeric complex with maximal molecular masses of ≈150 kDa or ≈265 kDa and ≈250 kDa, respectively.
source: Native gel electrophoresis and analytical gel filtration data revealed a rather fragile multimeric complex with maximal molecular masses of ≈150 kDa or ≈265 kDa (Figure 2B) and ≈250 kDa, respectively.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B and gel filtration analysis.

claim: Gel filtration profiles clearly indicate the partial dissociation of the Ldh-EtfAB complex into Ldh and EtfAB.
source: Gel filtration profiles clearly indicate the partial dissociation of the Ldh-EtfAB complex into Ldh and EtfAB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The heterologously produced Ldh-EtfAB complex shows similar biochemical properties as the protein isolated directly from A. woodii.
source: The heterologously produced Ldh-EtfAB complex shows similar biochemical properties as the protein isolated directly from A. woodii (Weghoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously published data cited.

claim: The Ldh-EtfAB complex catalyzes the confurcating Fdred-dependent lactate:NAD+ oxidoreductase reaction with a rate of 12.3±1.8 U/mg.
source: It catalyzes the confurcating Fdred-dependent lactate:NAD+ oxidoreductase reaction with a rate of 12.3±1.8 U/mg and the bifurcating pyruvate-dependent NADH:Fdox oxidoreductase reaction with a rate of 1.2±0.2 U/mg.
evidence: This is based on experimental kinetic measurements.

claim: The Ldh-EtfAB complex catalyzes the bifurcating pyruvate-dependent NADH:Fdox oxidoreductase reaction with a rate of 1.2±0.2 U/mg.
source: It catalyzes the confurcating Fdred-dependent lactate:NAD+ oxidoreductase reaction with a rate of 12.3±1.8 U/mg and the bifurcating pyruvate-dependent NADH:Fdox oxidoreductase reaction with a rate of 1.2±0.2 U/mg.
evidence: This is based on experimental kinetic measurements.

claim: FBEC activity was optimal between 25°C and 30°C.
source: FBEC activity was optimal between 25°C and 30°C (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FBEC activity decreased below 25°C or above 30°C by 40% or 20% and at 45°C to minor values.
source: It decreased below 25 or above 30°C by 40 or 20% and at 45°C to minor values.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Ldh-EtfAB complex had the highest FBEC activity at pH 7.
source: The Ldh-EtfAB complex had the highest FBEC activity at pH 7 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A decrease of the FBEC activity to 50% could be observed at pH 6 and 8 and inactivity at pH 5 and 10.
source: A decrease of the FBEC activity to 50% could be observed at pH 6 and 8 and inactivity at pH 5 and 10.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Similar FBEC activities could be measured when separately produced Ldh and EtfAB were added together, demonstrating the stability of the individual components and their capability to assemble.
source: Similar FBEC activities could be measured, when separately produced Ldh (data not shown) and EtfAB (separated in the gel filtration column) were added together, which demonstrate the stability of the individual components and their capability to assemble.
evidence: This is based on experimental kinetic measurements with reconstituted complex.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the Ldh-EtfAB complex was determined from a sample cross-linked with bis(sulfosuccinimidyl)suberate (BS3).
source: The cryo-EM structure of the fragile Ldh-EtfAB complex from A. woodii was determined from a sample cross-linked with bis(sulfosuccinimidyl)suberate (BS3), because multiple attempts without cross-linking failed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used for structure determination.

claim: Multiple attempts to determine the cryo-EM structure without cross-linking failed.
source: The cryo-EM structure of the fragile Ldh-EtfAB complex from A. woodii was determined from a sample cross-linked with bis(sulfosuccinimidyl)suberate (BS3), because multiple attempts without cross-linking failed.
evidence: This is a description of experimental challenges encountered.

claim: From 9,788 micrographs collected and 674,283 particles extracted a twofold-averaged density map at a mean resolution of 2.43 Å was calculated.
source: From 9,788 micrographs collected and 674,283 particles extracted a twofold-averaged density map at a mean resolution of 2.43 Å was calculated (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 1) using Relion (Scheres, 2012).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data processing as shown in Table 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The local resolution of the cryo-EM map ranges from 2.3 Å for the Ldh core to 3.1 Å for a peripheral EtfA region.
source: The local resolution ranges from 2.3 Å for the Ldh core to 3.1 Å for a peripheral EtfA region (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on local resolution analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The EM density was only disordered for the N-terminal Fd domain (2-65) of EtfA, for which model building was impossible.
source: The EM density was only disordered for the N-terminal Fd domain (2-65) of EtfA, for which model building was impossible.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The polypeptide chain of all other structural parts could be largely traced with ARP/WARP.
source: The polypeptide chain of all other structural parts could be largely traced with ARP/WARP (Langer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the model building process.

claim: The cryo-EM density at the flavin binding sites is highly reliable.
source: In particular, the cryo-EM density at the flavin binding sites is highly reliable (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on inspection of the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Ldh-EtfAB complex was found as a heterohexamer composed of a Ldh dimer forming the core and two EtfAB modules peripherally associated.
source: The Ldh-EtfAB complex was found as a heterohexamer composed of a Ldh dimer forming the core and two EtfAB modules peripherally associated.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Exclusively, the Ldh subunits provide the interface between the two Ldh-EtfAB protomers.
source: Exclusively, the Ldh subunits provide the interface between the two Ldh-EtfAB protomers (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The active site regions of the two Ldh-EtfAB protomers are ca. 30 Å apart from each other and considered to operate independently.
source: The active site regions of the two Ldh-EtfAB protomers are ca. 30 Å apart from each other and considered to operate independently.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements and inference about functional independence.

claim: The obtained molecular mass of ca. 255 kDa complex agrees with the value derived from gel filtration and native PAGE analysis.
source: The obtained molecular mass of ca. 255 kDa complex agrees with the value derived from gel filtration and native PAGE analysis.
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural and biochemical data.

claim: The cryo-EM (Ldh-EtfAB)2 structure shows both Ldh-EtfAB protomers in the resting D (dehydrogenation-connected) state.
source: In accordance with the X-ray structures of the Bcd-EtfAB/CarCDE/Fix-EtfABCX complexes (Demmer et al., 2018; Demmer et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2021) the cryo-EM (Ldh-EtfAB)2 structure shows both Ldh-EtfAB protomers in the resting D (dehydrogenation-connected) state (Figure 5A), in which electrons are exchangeable between a-FAD and d-FAD.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5A and comparison with related structures.

claim: In the D state, electrons are exchangeable between a-FAD and d-FAD.
source: In accordance with the X-ray structures of the Bcd-EtfAB/CarCDE/Fix-EtfABCX complexes (Demmer et al., 2018; Demmer et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2021) the cryo-EM (Ldh-EtfAB)2 structure shows both Ldh-EtfAB protomers in the resting D (dehydrogenation-connected) state (Figure 5A), in which electrons are exchangeable between a-FAD and d-FAD.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement and comparison with related complexes.

claim: During the reaction cycle ET has to be adjusted between a-FAD and b-FAD implicating a rotation of the EtfAB shuttle domain toward the B (bifurcation-connected) state.
source: During the reaction cycle ET has also to be adjusted between a-FAD and b-FAD implicating a rotation of the EtfAB shuttle domain toward the B (bifurcation-connected) state.
evidence: This is inferred from mechanistic considerations and structural analysis.

claim: Analysis of the EM micrographs with the aim to find a small population in the B-state failed.
source: Analysis of the EM micrographs with the aim to find a small population in the B-state failed.
evidence: This is a description of an unsuccessful experimental attempt.

claim: Bifurcating oxidoreductase-EtfAB complexes are only experimentally trapped in the D-state therefore considered as stable resting conformation.
source: So far, bifurcating oxidoreductase-EtfAB complexes are only experimentally trapped in the D-state therefore considered as stable resting conformation.
evidence: This is based on the current state of structural knowledge in the field.

claim: In bifurcating oxidoreductase-EtfAB complexes the B-state appears to be short-living and experimentally difficult to trap.
source: In bifurcating oxidoreductase-EtfAB complexes the B-state appears to be short-living and experimentally difficult to trap.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of experimental structures in the B-state.

claim: A B-state of the Ldh-EtfAB complex was found by applying the EtfA sequence to AlphaFold2 and aligning the N-terminal domain of EtfA with the cryo-EM Ldh-EtfAB structure.
source: However, a B-state of the Ldh-EtfAB complex was, unexpectedly, found (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) by applying the EtfA sequence to the recently published Alphafold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) and aligning the the N-terminal domain of EtfA (domain 1) with the cryo-EM Ldh-EtfAB structure (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold2 as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The EtfAB shuttle domain swings ca. 75° from the D-state into a B-state position.
source: The EtfAB shuttle domain swings ca. 75° from the D-state into a B-state position (Figure 5—video 1) that deviates from the previously proposed one (Demmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the D-state and AlphaFold2-derived B-state structures.

claim: The B-state position deviates from the previously proposed one.
source: The EtfAB shuttle domain swings ca. 75° from the D-state into a B-state position (Figure 5—video 1) that deviates from the previously proposed one (Demmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously published model cited.

claim: In the D-state, a-FAD and d-FAD are 3.7 Å apart from each other.
source: The experimentally characterized D-state. The EtfAB shuttle domain (red) is spatially separated from the rigid EtfAB base (EtfA domain I in gold and EtfB domain III in brown) and attached to Ldh (green). a-FAD and d-FAD are 3.7 Å, a-FAD and b-FAD ca. 37 Å apart from each other.
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the D-state, a-FAD and b-FAD are ca. 37 Å apart from each other.
source: The experimentally characterized D-state. The EtfAB shuttle domain (red) is spatially separated from the rigid EtfAB base (EtfA domain I in gold and EtfB domain III in brown) and attached to Ldh (green). a-FAD and d-FAD are 3.7 Å, a-FAD and b-FAD ca. 37 Å apart from each other.
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the B-state, the shortest distance between the isoalloxazine rings of a-FAD and b-FAD is 11.8 Å.
source: The B-state. By combining the experimental EM data and Alphafold2 calculations a plausible B-state could be established for the first time. Starting from the D-state the EtfAB shuttle domain swings 75° to adjust an ET distance between a-FAD and b-FAD. The shortest distance between the isoalloxazine rings is 11.8 Å.
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the AlphaFold2-derived B-state model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Upon rotation from D-state to B-state, the contact to Ldh is largely lost while that to the EtfAB base is formed.
source: Upon rotation the contact to Ldh is largely lost while that to the EtfAB base is formed.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of the D-state and B-state shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ldh is built up of two domains: an N-terminal FAD domain (1-218) subdivided into two α + β subdomains, a cap domain (219-417), and an extended C-terminal arm (418-467) attached to the FAD domain.
source: Ldh is built up of two domains, an N-terminal FAD domain (1-218) subdivided into two α + β subdomains, a cap domain (219-417) characterized by an antiparallel β-sheet element and an extended C-terminal arm (418-467) attached to the FAD domain (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The fold of Ldh classifies it as a member of a flavoenzyme family with p-cresol methyl hydroxylase (CMH), vanillyl-alcohol oxidase, MurB and membrane-associated Ldh as prototypes.
source: This fold classifies Ldh as a member of a flavoenzyme family with p-cresol methyl hydroxylase (CMH) (Cunane et al., 2000), vanillyl-alcohol oxidase (Mattevi et al., 1997), MurB (Benson et al., 1997) and membrane-associated Ldh (Dym et al., 2000) as prototypes (Fraaije et al., 1998); their corresponding rms deviations from Ldh of A. woodii are 2.6 Å (1DIQ, 407 of 467 residues used), 2.6 Å (1AHU, 399 of 467), 3.5 Å (2MBR, 203 of 467) and 2.4 Å (1FOX, 371 of 467).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with related enzymes cited.

claim: The rms deviation between Ldh of A. woodii and p-cresol methyl hydroxylase is 2.6 Å (407 of 467 residues used).
source: This fold classifies Ldh as a member of a flavoenzyme family with p-cresol methyl hydroxylase (CMH) (Cunane et al., 2000), vanillyl-alcohol oxidase (Mattevi et al., 1997), MurB (Benson et al., 1997) and membrane-associated Ldh (Dym et al., 2000) as prototypes (Fraaije et al., 1998); their corresponding rms deviations from Ldh of A. woodii are 2.6 Å (1DIQ, 407 of 467 residues used), 2.6 Å (1AHU, 399 of 467), 3.5 Å (2MBR, 203 of 467) and 2.4 Å (1FOX, 371 of 467).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison calculations.

claim: Except for the membrane-associated Ldh, CMH-type flavoenzymes are homodimers.
source: Except for the membrane-associated Ldh CMH-type flavoenzymes are homodimers.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of related enzyme structures.

claim: D-FAD is embedded between the two α + β subdomains except for the isoalloxazine ring that protrudes beyond the FAD domain towards the cap domain.
source: D-FAD is embedded between the two α + β subdomains except for the isoalloxazine ring that protrudes beyond the FAD domain towards the cap domain.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The isoalloxazine ring of d-FAD is well accessible from bulk solvent.
source: Therefore, the isoalloxazine is well accessible from bulk solvent (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The substrate binding site of Ldh is essentially formed by Leu80, Arg328, Leu332, Glu344, Asp346, His377, His384, Tyr386, Glu422, and His423.
source: The substrate binding sites is essentially formed by Leu80, Arg328, Leu332, Glu344, Asp346, His377, His384, Tyr386, Glu422, and His423 directly or indirectly involved in lactate binding/oxidation (Figure 6B) and well conserved in the membrane-associated Ldh (Figure 6—source data 1; Dym et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6B and comparison with related enzymes.

claim: The substrate binding site residues are well conserved in the membrane-associated Ldh.

claim: The redox potentials of the electron carriers a-FAD and d-FAD should be lower in Ldh-EtfAB than in Bcd-EtfAB for ensuring a smooth ET.
source: For ensuring a smooth ET the redox potentials of the electron carriers a-FAD and d-FAD between b-FAD and lactate should be also lower in Ldh-EtfAB than in Bcd-EtfAB and thus their microenvironment substantially different (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is inferred from thermodynamic considerations and structural comparison.

claim: Glu37 and Glu139 are in van-der-Waals contact with the isoalloxazines of a-FAD and d-FAD.
source: Structural inspections of Ldh-EtfAB, indeed, reveal two acidic residues, Glu37 and Glu139, in van-der-Waals contact with the isoalloxazines of a-FAD and d-FAD, which are conserved in bifurcating Ldh but not in membrane-spanning Ldh and have no equivalent in Bcd-EtfAB (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 9B.
